rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to capture all 6 compounds within 42 min and map the full elution window. This should reveal whether any peaks are unretained or still elute in the high-organic hold, guiding later narrowing of the gradient window and slope tuning.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the objective is now to cut time while keeping every peak inside the gradient. The first and last peaks correspond to roughly phi_e about 0.13 and 0.43, so a narrower window with a shorter gradient should pull the last peak well earlier while leaving margin around the elution range.

We are very close to the ideal, with all pairs still far above 1.5, so the next step is to shorten the gradient one notch while keeping the successful phi window and temperature fixed. This directly tests whether the last peak can be brought under 10 min without sacrificing resolution.

CRF is already maxed, so this run probes how much more speed margin exists before resolution starts to approach the 1.5 threshold. Keeping the same window and temperature isolates the effect of steeper slope and may identify an even faster fully resolved method.

The same window remains comfortably overresolved even at 4 min, so the next logical test is the shortest allowed gradient. This checks whether the fastest possible method still keeps the weakest pair above R = 1.5, which would dominate method selection among the tied CRF = 1.000 runs.

At 2 min only the first pair fails, suggesting the method is too steep at the front end; lowering phi0 should spread the earliest peaks while keeping the fast run and the late peaks safely retained. This tests whether a wider low-organic start can recover R(1,2) above 1.5 without sacrificing the very short analysis time.

The limiting pair at 2 min appears relatively insensitive to the phi-window tweak, so it likely needs a selectivity change rather than more slope adjustment. Lowering temperature is the cleanest next probe to see whether pair 1/2 separates enough at the shortest gradient while still keeping all peaks well under 10 min.

At 2 min, lowering temperature to 25 C restored full resolution but likely with more retention than necessary. Testing 30 C should determine whether a slightly warmer setting still keeps the critical first pair above 1.5 while giving a faster max-CRF method.

The 2 min method remains fully resolved at 30 C, and the limiting pair is still comfortably above 1.5. Testing 35 C brackets the transition toward failure and may yield the fastest temperature that still preserves full-credit resolution.

The threshold lies between 35 C and 40 C for the critical first pair, so 45 C is not for optimization but to confirm the temperature dependence and sharpen the boundary. This helps establish that 35 C is likely the warmest robust fully resolved 2 min method in this window.

Since the first pair is the only failure at the fastest gradients, a slightly narrower phi window may soften the effective steepness while still covering the observed elution range. Lowering phi1 should also avoid overcompressing the early part of the run and could rescue full resolution at a warmer, faster condition.

Narrowing the window to phi1 = 0.60 almost rescued the critical first pair at 40 C, so combining that gentler slope with the better selectivity at 35 C is a strong candidate for a faster max-CRF method. This directly tests whether the shortest gradient can remain fully resolved with a slightly tighter window and moderately warm temperature.

The only limiting pair is the earliest one, and it may benefit from moving the start composition closer to its elution region rather than beginning overly weak. Raising phi0 while keeping the successful 2 min, 35 C condition tests whether the front pair gains selectivity or spacing without compromising the rest.

Raising phi0 to 0.15 retained full resolution and shortened the run, suggesting the method may still tolerate a stronger start. One more step to phi0 = 0.20 probes whether the earliest pair remains above 1.5 while pushing the fully resolved 2 min method even faster.

The front pair improved further at phi0 = 0.20, so another increase in starting organic may continue to sharpen the fastest fully resolved method. This tests the limit before the first peak approaches the unretained region while monitoring whether the critical pair stays above 1.5.

The method is still fully resolved and slightly faster at phi0 = 0.25, but the first peak is now quite early, so one more increase should define the practical limit. This checks whether further speed gains are possible before the first compound becomes effectively unretained or the critical pair starts to collapse.

phi0 = 0.25 appears near-optimal for speed while keeping the first pair safely resolved, and reducing phi1 by one step may trim late retention without pushing the first peak into the unretained zone. This tests whether the same fast front-end can be paired with a slightly tighter overall gradient window for an even shorter max-CRF run.

phi0 = 0.25 looks best for the critical early pair, and increasing phi1 by one step from the successful 0.65 method may pull the last peak slightly earlier without affecting the front much. This is a targeted speed optimization within the already validated fully resolved 2 min, 35 C region.

Increasing phi1 to 0.70 preserved full resolution and dramatically shortened the last peak, so one more step upward is the most direct test for an even faster fully resolved method. The key risk remains the first pair, which still has some margin at R = 1.69.

The 2 min, 35 C method remains fully resolved at phi1 = 0.75 with the critical first pair still above threshold, so pushing phi1 one more step is the cleanest remaining speed optimization. This should reveal whether there is still room to shorten the latest peaks before pair 1/2 drops below R = 1.5.

phi1 = 0.80 places the critical pair exactly at the apparent resolution threshold, so one final increase will test whether this is the true edge of full resolution. This brackets the fastest viable method and confirms whether injection 20 is the shortest safe choice.

Injection 20 appears to sit right on the resolution edge, so lowering phi0 one step while keeping phi1 = 0.80 should give the critical first pair a bit more retention and safety margin with only a small effect on total time. This tests whether the same very fast endpoint can be made more robust without losing the 2 min fully resolved performance.

Injection 20 is the fastest full-resolution method found, but it sits exactly at the threshold for the first pair; dropping temperature one step should add robustness while keeping the same very short gradient and high phi1. This tests whether a slightly cooler version remains nearly as fast but with a clearer safety margin on the critical pair.

At 30 C the critical pair regained comfortable margin at phi1 = 0.80, so increasing phi1 to 0.85 could deliver an even faster fully resolved method than injection 20. This is the most informative remaining edge test because it combines the stronger selectivity of 30 C with the shorter late elution seen at higher phi1.

Injection 24 is currently the fastest fully resolved method, and the critical first pair still has useful margin at R = 1.63. The final injection should therefore test one last increase in phi1 to see whether an even shorter max-CRF method is possible before that pair drops below 1.5.
